overview: Stability and minimizing total rank are different objectives. In the printed complete three-by-three profile, AY/BZ/CX uniquely minimizes aggregate rank at 10 but BX blocks it. AY/BX/CZ is uniquely stable, with total 11. Rank numbers are an invented puzzle score, not a measurement of real happiness.

With strict incomplete two-side lists, only mutually listed pairs are acceptable, every acceptable partner is better than being unpaired, and a stable matching has no allowed pair both preferring one another. Perfect pairing need not exist even with equal sides. Nevertheless all stable matchings match exactly the same objects; partners can change while the unpaired set cannot. A finite alternating-path argument proves this invariant.

Removing the two-side restriction changes existence. Four objects in one group have only three perfect pairings. The left printed profile blocks all three; the right has stable AB/CD. Thus the complete strict two-side existence theorem cannot be applied unchanged to one-group roommates.

Children investigate score versus stability, omitted choices, and one-group existence: three directions. Grades 2-3 can build/check visible pairs; Grades 4-5 can certify optima, nonexistence and the matched-set invariant. The real gate is retaining current partners and checking both wishes from one unchanged state. Search supplies examples; a complete blocker catalog or alternating-path contradiction supplies an explanation.
readiness: Fixed tables: KK11 / 3333 / 445, with one anchored adult each. Use one investigation and its brief launch per table visit. Adults read/record while children own the mathematical choices. Entry needs short ordered lists, fixed current partners and both preference checks. No separate K-1 route is forced; an oral four-token trial is optional only after this gate is retained.
P1 adds rank sums through 15; P2 adds the unpaired state. P3 uses one group, not circles paired only with squares. P4's universal explanation is readiness-dependent return work.
materials: Per table: labeled artificial tokens A,B,C,X,Y,Z; six reusable preference strips and six blanks; removable pairing links; rank cards 1-3; visible unpaired spaces; pencils and paper. For P3 supply four same-style tokens A-D and four strips. Large labels about 20 mm help pointing. Do not rank real children's friendships or desirability.

Prepare the printed lists and preserve omissions genuinely; a missing choice is not tied last. Allowed edges require both names. Keep current pairs and preferences unchanged while checking blockers, and keep unpaired objects visible. About 10-15 minutes to prepare reusable strips; independent child retention of the simultaneous checks remains untested.
launch: After handling tokens, use the final visual: current UP and VQ, V's list P,Q and P's list V,U, with current partners boxed. V prefers P to Q and P prefers V to U, so VP blocks. Do not change a pair between the two checks. For P2 show an unacceptable omitted edge; for P3 explicitly remove the two-side rule.
route: Allow a 2-3 minute launch and 20-35 minutes for P1 or P2. Return for P3's contrasting existence cases or P4's general invariant. These timings are proposals. Retain a list profile and a checked reference matching; allow children to stay with one investigation instead of finishing all four pages.

investigations.title: Lowest score is not always stable
investigations.entry: Build candidates and attach their two rank numbers to each pair. Grades 2-3 can pool the six cases; older children can certify both minima. Allow 20-30 minutes. Rank score and a blocker are separate records about the same unchanged matching.
solution: All six perfect matchings, totals and full blockers: AX/BY/CZ: 15, AY/AZ/CY; AX/BZ/CY: 13, AY/BX; AY/BX/CZ: 11, none; AY/BZ/CX: 10, BX; AZ/BX/CY: 11, AY; AZ/BY/CX: 12, AY. Fixing A's partner then matching the two others gives exactly six, so this is complete.

The unique aggregate minimum AY/BZ/CX scores 10. B ranks X second ahead of current Z third, and X ranks B first ahead of current C third: BX blocks. The unique stable result AY/BX/CZ has pair scores 2,3,6 totaling 11, hence is also the lowest stable total. Maximizing a different notion of collective benefit is not what stability alone guarantees.
hints: Let a child compare B/X's wishes in the lowest-score reference before checking every other potential pair. For completeness, offer movable matching links rather than prescribing a written enumeration order.
extensions: Why can a low aggregate total conceal a mutually preferred switch? In the printed minimum AY/BZ/CX, forming BX breaks BZ and CX, leaving C and Z unpaired until re-paired; AY stays. Pairing CZ completes AY/BX/CZ. A blocker test and a complete rearrangement are different questions. Keep artificial scores and real preferences conceptually separate.
investigations.notes: A unilateral wish is not enough. Adult reading support can help; adults making all blocker decisions would remove the investigation.

investigations.title: Partners can change; matched objects cannot
investigations.entry: P2 uses small omitted-choice profiles and visible unpaired objects. P4 lets children design lists and seek a counterexample. Allow 20-40 minutes; the general proof can be a separate upper return conversation using alternating colored links.
solution: P2 first profile: AX is uniquely stable, leaving B and Y unpaired. Empty matching is blocked by AX; BX leaves A unpaired and is blocked by AX because X prefers A. Y has no allowed edge. Equal side sizes do not force everyone to pair.

Second profile: exactly AX/BY and AY/BX are stable, both leaving C,Z unpaired. Z has no edge. If CY were used, one of A/B would be unpaired because only X remains; that free object and Y block, since Y ranks A and B ahead of C. Without C matched, neither A nor B can stay unpaired: a free acceptable X/Y, or the receiver's preference for the unpaired object over its current partner, creates a blocker. Both A/B full alternatives pass both-sided checks. Partners differ, unpaired objects do not.

P4's requested counterexample does not exist under the shared conventions. Suppose p0 is unpaired in stable M but paired with r0 in stable N. M-stability forces r0 to have an M-partner p1 preferred to p0. N-stability forces p1 to have an N-partner r1 preferred to r0, otherwise p1/r0 block N. M-stability now forces r1 to have an M-partner p2 preferred to p1, and so on.

The M/N links form an alternating path beginning at an unmatched endpoint. It cannot repeat: a matching gives at most one edge of each type, so any repeated alternating component would be a cycle disconnected from that endpoint. It cannot terminate without the blocking pair just forced. Finiteness contradicts endless continuation. Exchange M/N and then the sides to prove equality of matched sets. Strict preferences, mutual acceptability and acceptable-above-unpaired are essential; failed counterexample search alone is not this proof.
hints: Keep unpaired tokens in view. When CY is tried, ask which object now has no partner and whether Y prefers it. For P4, preserve two proposed stable matchings side by side and follow alternating links from an object claimed to change status.
extensions: Starting from the first profile, remove A-X from both lists. BX is now uniquely stable, leaving A,Y unpaired. Changing the profile can change unmatched objects; the theorem compares matchings of one fixed profile, not different profiles.
investigations.notes: Zero-choice objects remain participants. An omitted acceptable relation must be absent from the allowed-edge set; do not use an unacceptable pair to fill an empty place.

investigations.title: One group may have no stable pairing
investigations.entry: Four identical-style tokens permit every within-group pair. Keep one candidate matching fixed while testing both wishes. Allow 15-30 minutes. A child can explain nonexistence by exhausting three drawings, without a matching algorithm.
solution: There are exactly three perfect pairings: choose A's partner B,C or D, and the remaining two must pair. In the left profile AB/CD is blocked by BC; AC/BD by AB; AD/BC by AC. Every candidate therefore fails, proving no stable perfect pairing exists.

In the right profile AB/CD consists of two mutual first-choice pairs and is stable. AC/BD is blocked by AB and CD. AD/BC is blocked by AB, AC and CD. Thus AB/CD is uniquely stable. Some one-group profiles work and others do not; the left example refutes a universal existence claim for this changed model.

The base deferred-acceptance theorem assumes two disjoint sides with every pair crossing sides. It does not imply a stable solution for this one-group question. Here perfect pairing is required; leaving everyone unpaired is not a permitted answer.
hints: After a genuine attempt, fix A-B and check the remaining possible mutual wishes. Use the three matching boards to establish completeness; do not interpret an algorithm's failure as a nonexistence proof.
extensions: Any one-group profile with all objects organized into mutual first-choice pairs has a stable matching of those pairs: no object prefers anyone else. The right profile illustrates that sufficient construction.
investigations.notes: Use fixed artificial labels and the same preference strips throughout an instance. Repeatedly updating partners while testing blockers changes the reference and can hide the intended contradiction.

sources: Current Week 27 base packets/guide establish strict complete two-side stability. The base outline cites Pass and Halpern, A Course in Networks and Markets, Chapter 14 sections 14.1-14.3 for that model. No new source-body reading or attribution of these new examples is claimed. The score and roommate catalogs and incomplete-list proof are independently supplied here.

Rozhkovskaya, Math Circles for Elementary School Students, Introduction: Berkeley 2009 (OEBPS/part0010.xhtml), actually reports individual adult support. Our visible strips and anchored adult help are proposed adaptations. Week 13 allowed-edge capacity is related but lacks these preference/blocker conditions.
verification: The fresh student math critic recomputed every score/blocker, both partial-matching profiles and both roommate profiles, and independently checked incomplete-list examples plus the general alternating-path proof. Final revision supplied the actual ordered input strips in the blocking visual; guide answers use the revised final packet.

The final guide received a separate independent mathematical review. Both final PDFs were rendered and inspected and passed a clean extracted-source ZIP rebuild. See release-validation.json in the editable source package. No physical procedure, staffing success or independent child retention has been rehearsed. All materials are unpiloted.
observations: Record investigations used, actual preference profiles, retained matchings and a useful continuation.

Observe whether both checks are made from one unchanged reference, missing choices remain unacceptable, unpaired tokens stay visible, and a child controls the blocker decision. Separate those observations from readiness hypotheses.
